title: Turning an Example into Your Code
summary: Why documentation examples are not production code - what they leave out on purpose - and a dependable routine for adapting one - run it unchanged, understand every line against the reference, make it a function, add every error path the reference describes, release resources on every path, and test the edges.

cards.q: Why run an example unchanged before adapting it?
cards.a:
So later problems are known to come from your changes

Running it first confirms it works in your environment. If it then breaks after your edits, you know where to look.

cards.q: An example calls `read` once. When is that not enough?
cards.a:
When a read can return fewer bytes than requested

Many read functions may return less than you asked for, for example from a pipe or a socket, or near the end. Real code loops until it has everything or reaches the end.

cards.q: How do you make sure a handle is closed on every error path?
cards.a:
Wrap it in an RAII object whose destructor closes it

A destructor runs on every way out of the scope, early returns and exceptions included, so no path can forget the close.

cards.q: What is wrong with `std::string(buffer, n)` when `n` can be -1?
cards.a:
-1 becomes a huge `size_t`, so it reads far past the buffer

The length parameter is unsigned, so -1 converts to the largest `size_t`. Check the error value before using it as a length.
